results.result: Experimental crosses of loach species across a phylogenetic spectrum revealed a continuum of reproductive outcomes, with most crosses producing sterile males and asexually reproducing females, while closely related species produced sexual hybrids and distant species produced sterile or inviable hybrids.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C76, C77, C78, C83, and C85 collectively describe the main experimental finding showing a reproductive continuum. The data from 19 F1 hybrid families across 12 species combinations (C39, C40) with cytological analysis (C42-C61) provide strong converging evidence for this pattern.

results.result: Hybrid females produced a small proportion of oocytes with premeiotically duplicated genomes that could complete meiosis and form clonal eggs, while most oocytes with unduplicated genomes experienced aberrant chromosome pairing and were arrested at meiotic checkpoints.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C51, C54, C55, C59-C61, C102-C104 are supported by detailed cytological analysis of pachytene and diplotene oocytes showing ~0.7% endoreplication at pachytene (C62) but 100% at diplotene (C66), with immunofluorescence and chromosome spread data (Figures 3-4) demonstrating aberrant pairing in non-duplicated cells and normal pairing in duplicated cells.

results.result: Hybrid males were sterile due to either failure to enter meiosis (TB and PS hybrids) or aberrant chromosome pairing during meiosis, with flow cytometry showing absence of haploid cells and histology revealing defective testes, except for NP hybrids between closely related species which showed normal pairing.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52, C107, C113-C114 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including flow cytometry (C48, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), histology (C50, Figure 3—figure supplement 4), and chromosome analysis (C51, C52, Figure 3) showing 244 analyzed cells with aberrant pairing in most hybrids except NP hybrids with 36 cells showing full pairing.

results.result: The number of bivalents formed in hybrid meiocytes was negatively correlated with both karyotype dissimilarity (AKD index) and genetic distance between parental species, with males forming significantly fewer bivalents than females.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75, C108-C109, C119 are supported by GLMM statistical analysis showing significant negative correlations (z=-5.86, p<10⁻⁸ for AKD; z=-3.73, p<10⁻³ for genetic distance; z=-4.54, p<10⁻⁵ for sex effect) based on analysis of 244 male and 665 female pachytene cells (C51, C57).

results.result: Premeiotic genome endoreplication occurred at very low frequency (~0.7%) in F1 hybrid females with no significant differences among crosses, but was significantly higher than in parental species (0%) and lower than in natural clones (~6%), with endoreplicated cells able to progress to diplotene while non-duplicated cells arrested at pachytene.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C65-C69, C121-C122 are supported by statistical comparisons using GLM showing no differences among F1 crosses (p=0.59, C63), significant difference from parental species (p=0.00615, C68) based on 792 analyzed oocytes showing 0% endoreplication (C69), and significant difference from natural clones (p<10⁻⁵, C65), with the pachytene-diplotene contrast explained by selective progression (C66-C67).

results.result: Asexual gametogenesis emerged commonly across multiple independent species pairs (7 of 11 experimental crosses, 10 of 18 including literature), appearing tightly linked to hybrid sterility and constituting an inherent part of the extended speciation continuum, contradicting the view that asexual lineage origins are rare.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C22, C90-C91, C93-C94, C126 are supported by the experimental data showing widespread emergence of asexual gametogenesis (C88-C89) across phylogenetically diverse crosses (C39-C40), with the pattern not depending on any particular parental genome (C90) and occurring directly in F1 generation (C94), though the broader evolutionary interpretation (C9, C22) involves some inference beyond the direct experimental evidence.

results.result: All F1 females capable of clonal gametogenesis employed the same cytogenetic mechanism—premeiotic genome endoreplication—which allows hybrids to overcome chromosome pairing problems by producing identical chromosome copies that can pair during meiosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96, C17-C18 are supported by cytological analysis showing identical mechanism across all clonal F1 females (C61, C95) with properly formed bivalents in endoreplicated cells (C54, C61, Figure 4d), consistent with previous observations in natural asexual vertebrates (multiple citations in C95-C96), though the mechanistic explanation for why this pathway is favored (C96) involves some inference.

results.result: Karyotype divergence (AKD index) significantly increased with genetic divergence among parental species (Mantel test, r=0.338, p=0.0261), though the correlation was not always linear because some phylogenetically distant species possess morphologically similar karyotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are supported by statistical analysis (Mantel test with stated parameters) and karyotype data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1) showing the relationship between AKD and SNP distances, with the non-linearity explained by convergent karyotype evolution in Bicanestrinia and Adriatic groups (C38).

results.result: Eight focal species were crossed in 12 combinations producing viable progeny of both sexes in all attempted crosses, resulting in 19 F1 hybrid families with no significant deviations from equal sex ratios.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 describe the experimental design and basic outcomes, supported by Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2, with statistical testing showing no sex ratio bias (binomial test, all P>0.25 after correction, C41). This provides the foundation for subsequent analyses.

results.result: All F1 hybrids contained germ cells organized in clusters similar to sexual fish, with most showing formation of synaptonemal complexes indicating meiocyte presence, except PS and TB males which lacked meiocytes; parental species showed normal gametogenesis with 24-25 synaptonemal complexes and haploid cells in flow cytometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 are supported by immunofluorescence staining with anti-Vasa and anti-SYCP3 antibodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), flow cytometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a), and histology (Figure 3—figure supplement 4a), with analysis of 852 cells from parental species (C45) providing baseline controls for comparison.

results.result: OB and NP hybrids showed exceptional patterns with diplotene oocytes containing only 25 bivalents suggesting normal meiosis with pairing between orthologous chromosomes, representing sexual reproduction in hybrids between closely related or karyotypically similar species.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C58, C82 are supported by cytological analysis showing 25 bivalents in both pachytene and diplotene stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d, Figure 4—figure supplement 3f), consistent with normal meiotic pairing, though the inference about orthologous vs. homologous pairing (C56) is reasonable but not directly proven.

results.result: Karyotype divergence has an indirect impact on asexual reproduction: asexuality tends to occur in hybrids with diverged parental karyotypes that prevent orthologous pairing in non-duplicated cells, while karyotype similarity allows completion of meiosis and sexual reproduction even in phylogenetically distant species.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80, C117-C118, C120, C124, C130 are supported by the correlation between AKD and bivalent formation (C71-C72), the observation that OB hybrids between distant but karyotypically similar species can form full bivalent sets (C120, Figure 5), and the low endoreplication frequency even in natural clones (~6%, C123), though the mechanistic interpretation involves inference from correlational data.

results.result: Fundamental differences exist in chromosome pairing mechanisms between spermatogenesis and oogenesis, with evidence that premeiotic endoreplication may rely on female-specific gonadal environment rather than genetic sex determination, based on transplantation experiments showing male germ cells can undergo endoreplication in female gonads.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are supported by the sex-specific differences in bivalent formation (C73, C108-C109) and citation to transplantation experiments (Tichopád et al., 2022, C111), though the mechanistic interpretation (C112) is inferential and the transplantation data is from a cited study rather than presented in this manuscript.

results.result: Analogous patterns of aberrant chromosome pairing were observed in non-duplicated oocytes of most hybrid females, indicating that problems in bivalent formation have detrimental impacts on meiosis in both male and female loach hybrids.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 are supported by cytological analysis showing similar aberrant pairing patterns in both sexes (C59, Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), though females differ in having a rescue mechanism through endoreplication (C103-C104), making the conclusion about detrimental impact valid but with sex-specific outcomes.

results.result: Successful establishment of hybrid clones under natural conditions is likely restricted by multiple selective filters: crosses must produce sufficient unreduced gametes while preventing formation of reduced gametes from non-duplicated meiocytes, potentially requiring sufficiently diverged karyotypes to ensure improper pairing in non-duplicated cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C127, C131-C134 represent hypotheses proposed to reconcile experimental findings with the rarity of natural asexual lineages. While the experimental data support the premises (low endoreplication frequency, karyotype effects on pairing), the proposed selective filtering mechanism (C127, C131-C132) is speculative and not directly tested. The hypothesis is logical but requires additional experiments or population-level data for validation.

results.result: The selected parental species represent three distinct phylogenetic lineages from Europe (Cobitis sensu stricto, Adriatic, and Bicanestrinia) that diverged 17-20 Mya, with diverse karyotypes having 48-50 chromosomes, providing a phylogenetic framework spanning from closely related species (diverged ~1 Mya) to distant lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35, C25-C29 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) based on exome-wide SNP data, karyotype analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1), and citations to published phylogenetic studies (Perdices et al., 2016; Majtánová et al., 2016; Janko et al., 2018), providing well-established context for the experimental crosses.

results.result: Diploid and polyploid hybrids including gynogenetic asexual lineages have been reported in Cobitidae, where clonal eggs require sperm activation but eliminate the male genome, with only hybrid females producing unreduced gametes via premeiotic genome endoreplication while males are sterile.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 describe established knowledge about natural Cobitidae hybrid systems, supported by multiple citations (Yamashita et al., 1990; Fyon et al., 2023; Morishima et al., 2008; Kim and Lee, 1995; Choleva et al., 2012; Dedukh et al., 2020, 2021) and illustrated in Figure 1, providing important biological context for interpreting the experimental results.

results.result: No significant maternal effects were observed in reciprocal crosses (ET vs TE, OE vs EO), allowing pooling of data across cross directions.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by comparison of reciprocal crosses, though the statistical test used is not explicitly stated. This is an important methodological finding that justifies pooling data, but the lack of detailed statistical reporting for this comparison is a minor limitation.

results.result: Production of unreduced gametes was observed in 7 of 11 experimentally crossed species pairs and in 10 of 18 species pairs when including literature reports and natural hybrids.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by the experimental data (Figure 2) and literature compilation (Figure 6), providing a quantitative assessment of the frequency of asexual gametogenesis emergence, though the denominator for 'success rate' depends on which crosses are considered viable attempts.

results.result: Similar observations of rare endoreplicated oogonia have been reported from several natural and experimental hybrid vertebrates, suggesting that even successfully established hybrid asexuals usually contain only a minor proportion of oogonia undergoing clonal gametogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 are supported by citations to studies of other hybrid systems (Dedukh et al., 2022a, 2021; Iwai et al., 2011; Newton et al., 2016), providing comparative context that strengthens the generality of the findings, though the inference about 'successfully established' asexuals (C106) extends beyond the direct evidence.

results.result: While asexual reproduction can be triggered by interspecific hybridization, its emergence is supposedly rare according to prevailing views, with most knowledge coming from natural lineages rather than experimental crosses, and origins often traced to single or few hybridization events.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C23-C24, C125 represent the prevailing view in the field that the manuscript challenges. These are well-supported by citations (Stöck et al., 2010; Choleva et al., 2012; Neaves and Baumann, 2011) and provide important context for the significance of the experimental findings, though the manuscript's data suggest this view requires revision.

results.result: The speciation continuum concept and balance hypothesis provide theoretical frameworks for understanding hybrid reproductive outcomes, with the extended speciation continuum explicitly linking asexual reproduction emergence to speciation, and the balance hypothesis proposing that asexuality emerges in a favorable evolutionary window of genetic divergence.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C16, C19-C21 describe established theoretical frameworks from the literature (Shaw and Mullen, 2014; Stankowski and Ravinet, 2021; Moritz et al., 1989; Stöck et al., 2021) that provide conceptual context for interpreting the experimental results. These are well-cited background concepts rather than new findings.

results.result: In hybrids between far-distant species pairs (EB, TB), sterility occurred in both sexes, while the most common asymmetric pattern (sterile males, asexual females) occurred in crosses with divergences up to ~17-20 Mya; an intermediate pattern with both reduced and unreduced female gametes occurred in TP hybrids between closely related species (~1 Mya divergence).
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C86-C87 are supported by the experimental data (Figure 2, Figure 6) and citations to natural hybrid complexes (Itono et al., 2006; Dedukh et al., 2020, 2021; Janko et al., 2018), describing the range of reproductive outcomes across the phylogenetic spectrum, though the TP hybrid data appears to be from cited literature rather than new experiments.

results.result: Asexual gametogenesis has been observed in experimental F1 progeny of several other vertebrate species.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is supported by citation (Iwai et al., 2011) and provides comparative context suggesting the phenomenon may be more general across vertebrates, though this is based on literature rather than new data and the extent of the phenomenon in other taxa remains unclear.

results.result: Cell cycle regulation is particularly sensitive to stress and perturbations, with interspecific hybridization potentially acting as such a stimulus, and aberrations leading to endoreplication may be more common because they require fewer accumulated incompatibilities than other routes to unreduced gamete production.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 are supported by citations (Rotelli et al., 2019; Moritz et al., 1989), but C99 is speculative ('it is possible that') without direct experimental evidence. The hypothesis is plausible given the data showing widespread endoreplication, but the mechanistic claim about relative ease of different pathways requires experimental testing.

results.result: Analysis of hundreds of gonocytes from sexual females showed no genome endoreplication, and no autotriploid specimens were found among hundreds of genotyped C. elongatoides, C. taenia, and their progeny, arguing against spontaneous unreduced gamete production in parental species.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 are supported by data from this study and previous work (Dedukh et al., 2020, 2021; Janko et al., 2012; Tichopád et al., 2022), with 792 analyzed oocytes showing 0% endoreplication (C69), providing important negative controls that strengthen the conclusion that endoreplication is hybrid-specific rather than a background phenomenon in parental species.

results.result: Even the most widespread natural clones possessed only ~6% endoreplicated oogonia.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 is based on previously published data (implied from C65, C122) and provides important context for interpreting the F1 hybrid data (~0.7% endoreplication), suggesting that even successful natural clones maintain relatively low frequencies of endoreplication, though the source of this specific value should be more explicitly cited.

results.result: The balance hypothesis suggests unreduced gamete production requires some genetic divergence to alter hybrid cell cycles toward endoreplication, yet most meiocytes of asexual hybrids do not undergo endoreplication.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 describe a tension between theoretical predictions and empirical observations. C128 is supported by citations to the balance hypothesis (Moritz et al., 1989; Janko et al., 2018; Stöck et al., 2010), while C129 is supported by citations to empirical studies (Dedukh et al., 2022a, 2021; Iwai et al., 2011; Newton et al., 2016) and the current data (C62), highlighting an important paradox that motivates the proposed resolution (C131-C132).

results.result: The production of unreduced gametes may be surprisingly easy to trigger in hybrids of distantly related lineages, and conclusions about asexuality evolution should be based on experimental crosses rather than only natural asexuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 represent key conclusions from the study, supported by the widespread emergence of asexual gametogenesis in experimental crosses (C88-C89) contrasting with the rarity of natural asexual lineages (C23, C125), though the recommendation (C136) is a methodological prescription rather than an empirical finding.

results.result: C. ohridana has 2n=50 chromosomes with 20 meta-/submetacentric and 30 subtelo-/acrocentric chromosomes, while C. tanaitica has 2n=50 chromosomes with 40 meta-/submetacentric and 10 subtelo-/acrocentric chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C138 are supported by karyotype analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, providing specific examples of karyotype diversity among parental species with the same chromosome number but different morphologies, illustrating why AKD rather than just chromosome number is important for measuring karyotype divergence.

results.result: Hybrid inviability has been reported in crosses between distant loach species.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by citation (Suzuki, 1957) and provides context for one extreme of the reproductive continuum, though no new inviability data is presented in this study as all attempted crosses produced viable progeny (C40).

results.result: The study found that gametogenic pathways in F1 hybrids followed a continuum from sexual reproduction in closely related species to sterility/inviability in distant species, with most crosses producing sterile males and asexually reproducing females. This pattern occurred across a relatively wide window of genetic divergence.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the evidence is 'compelling' and highlights 'the production of clonal gametes is common across hybrids between closely to moderately divergent sexual species.' Reviewer 2 notes this is 'a substantial advance' and praises the 'sound' analyses. Reviewer 3 calls the experiments 'rigorous' and the evidence 'strong.'

results.result: Hybrid gametes from both males and females usually experienced problems in chromosome pairing during meiosis, with aberrant pairing patterns including univalents, bivalents, and multivalents observed in most F1 hybrids. These meiotic defects led to arrest at meiotic checkpoints.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without question. Reviewer 3 specifically notes 'the authors provide strong evidence that premeiotic genome endoreplication is the mechanism behind asexually-reproducing females' and that meiosis arrests in males, implicitly accepting the chromosome pairing defects as the underlying cause. The cytogenetic work is described as 'beautiful' by Reviewer 2.

results.result: Hybrid females produced a small proportion of oocytes (~0.7% at pachytene, 100% at diplotene) with premeiotically duplicated genomes through endoreplication, enabling these cells to form normal bivalents and complete meiosis to produce clonal eggs, while non-duplicated oocytes arrested at pachytene.
results.evaluation: This mechanism is explicitly endorsed by all reviewers. Reviewer 3 states 'the authors provide strong evidence that premeiotic genome endoreplication is the mechanism behind asexually-reproducing females.' Reviewer 1 describes the molecular cytogenetic experiments as 'rigorous' and 'compelling.' The differential survival of endoreplicated vs. non-endoreplicated cells is accepted as demonstrated.

results.result: The incidence of genome endoreplication was significantly higher in F1 hybrids than in parental species, where no duplications were observed among 792 analyzed oocytes. This demonstrates that endoreplication is specifically triggered by hybridization rather than being a background phenomenon in sexual species.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly affirms this finding: 'the authors did not observe a single incidence of genome duplication in any of the parental species among a large number of surveyed oocytes,' and finds this evidence 'convincing that this phenomenon is a consequence of combining two divergent genomes in an F1 hybrid female.' This control comparison is critical to the main conclusion.

results.result: The production of unreduced gametes was observed in 7 out of 11 experimental crosses (10 out of 18 including literature), occurring relatively commonly across independent species pairs. This suggests that asexual gametogenesis arises more frequently in F1 hybrids than the rarity of natural asexual lineages would suggest.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 identifies this as 'a key finding' that 'the precondition for asexual reproduction - the formation of unreduced gametes - is not unusual among hybrid females, so that we have to consider other factors to explain the rarity of asexual species.' Reviewer 1 notes this work 'will be of broad interest to evolutionary biologists' by highlighting the 'potential for asexuality to evolve in hybrids during a relatively wide window of species divergence.'

results.result: The number of properly formed bivalents in hybrid pachytene cells was negatively correlated with both karyotype dissimilarity (AKD) and genetic distance between parental species, with males forming significantly fewer bivalents than females.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these statistical findings without critique. Reviewer 2 specifically notes 'the analyses are sound' and highlights that 'this work also highlights a previously overlooked effect of chromosome organisation on speciation.' The sex-specific differences are implicitly accepted as part of the overall pattern described.

results.result: The emergence of asexual gametogenesis appears tightly linked to hybrid sterility and constitutes part of the extended speciation continuum. However, successful establishment of asexual lineages in nature likely requires additional selective filters beyond the initial production of unreduced gametes, including appropriate karyotype divergence to prevent formation of reduced gametes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse this conceptual framework. Reviewer 1 notes the work provides 'important insights' by 'highlighting the potential for asexuality to evolve in hybrids during a relatively wide window of species divergence.' Reviewer 2 states this is 'a major unresolved issue in evolutionary biology' and that the findings require 'consider[ing] other factors to explain the rarity of asexual species.' The link to the speciation continuum is described as 'sensible' by Reviewer 2.

results.result: All F1 females capable of clonal gametogenesis employed the same cytogenetic mechanism (premeiotic genome endoreplication), suggesting that gametogenic perturbations induced by hybridization are canalized into a similar developmental pathway.
results.evaluation: This finding is accepted by reviewers as part of the overall mechanism. Reviewer 3 notes the evidence is 'strong' for premeiotic genome endoreplication as the mechanism. The consistency of mechanism across different hybrid combinations supports the generality of the findings that reviewers praise.

results.result: Viable F1 progeny of both sexes were obtained from all 12 attempted species combinations (19 families total), with no significant sex ratio deviations. All hybrids contained germ cells organized in clusters, and most showed formation of synaptonemal complexes indicating meiocyte presence.
results.evaluation: These methodological results are implicitly accepted by all reviewers. Reviewer 1 describes the experiments as 'rigorous' and Reviewer 3 as 'impressively detailed.' The successful generation of hybrids across divergence levels is essential to the main findings that reviewers explicitly support.

results.result: Hybrid males lacked haploid cell populations characteristic of spermatids/spermatozoa, had defective testes with asynchronous germinal cell development, and exhibited two types of sterility: failure to transition to meiosis (TB, PS males) or aberrant chromosome pairing preventing progression to spermatids (most other males).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the overall characterization of hybrid sterility. Reviewer 3 notes the work shows 'meiosis arrests early in male hybrids' as part of the 'impressively detailed characterization of gametogenesis.' The flow cytometry and histological evidence is implicitly accepted through reviewers' endorsement of the overall conclusions.

results.result: NP hybrids (between closely related C. tanaitica and C. pontica) showed fully paired chromosomes during pachytene and presence of spermatid nuclei in males, while females showed normal meiosis. Similarly, OB females and TP hybrids showed patterns consistent with sexual reproduction or mixed reproductive modes.
results.evaluation: These exceptions to the general pattern are accepted as part of the continuum described. Reviewer 1 notes the work shows asexuality can arise 'between closely to moderately divergent sexual species,' implicitly accepting that very close relatives may remain sexual. The continuum concept that reviewers endorse requires these transitional cases.

results.result: The incidence of genome endoreplication at pachytene was very low (~0.7%) across all F1 hybrid females with no significant differences between crosses or reciprocal directions. Natural clones showed higher incidence (~6%) than experimental F1 hybrids, suggesting this trait may increase during evolutionary establishment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these quantitative findings without critique. The comparison with natural clones is part of the evidence Reviewer 3 finds 'convincing' for the hybrid origin of the mechanism. The low frequency at pachytene contrasting with 100% at diplotene supports the selective elimination model that reviewers implicitly endorse.

results.result: There are fundamental differences in pairing mechanisms between spermatogenesis and oogenesis, with evidence that initiation of premeiotic endoreplication may rely on female-specific gonadal environment rather than genetic sex determination, based on transplantation experiments showing male germ cells can undergo endoreplication in female gonads.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic insight is accepted as part of the overall findings. Reviewer 2 notes the work 'highlights a previously overlooked effect of chromosome organisation on speciation,' which encompasses these sex-specific differences. The transplantation evidence is cited without reviewer challenge.

results.result: The eight parental species represent three distinct phylogenetic lineages with diverse karyotypes (2n=48-50), and karyotype divergence (AKD) significantly increases with genetic divergence, though the correlation is not always linear due to some distant species having similar karyotypes.
results.evaluation: These characterization data are accepted by reviewers as the foundation for the experimental design. Reviewer 2 praises the approach of 'analysing meiotic processes in F1 hybrids for combinations of species spanning different levels of divergence,' implicitly endorsing the phylogenetic and karyotypic framework presented.

results.result: Asexuality tends to be observed in hybrids between species with substantially diverged karyotypes, while sexual reproduction requires more similar karyotypes. Karyotype divergence has a crucial but indirect impact on asexual reproduction by affecting chromosome pairing, with karyotypically similar hybrids able to complete meiosis sexually even if capable of producing some unreduced gametes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly highlights this finding: 'this work also highlights a previously overlooked effect of chromosome organisation on speciation.' The relationship between karyotype divergence and reproductive mode is central to the model that all reviewers endorse regarding why asexual lineages are rare in nature despite frequent production of unreduced gametes.

results.result: While asexual reproduction can be triggered by hybridization and was previously thought to be rare, the experimental data indicate that production of unreduced gametes may be surprisingly easy to trigger in hybrids. This suggests conclusions about asexuality evolution should be based on experimental crosses, not just natural asexuals.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion is strongly endorsed by all reviewers. Reviewer 2 calls it 'a key finding' that challenges previous assumptions. Reviewer 1 states the work 'will be of broad interest to evolutionary biologists' precisely because it reveals asexuality can arise more readily than previously thought. Reviewer 3 finds the evidence 'convincing' for this reinterpretation.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the core finding of a reproductive continuum with widespread clonal gamete production across hybrids. OpenEval cites 19 F1 families and cytological evidence (C39-C61), while peer reviewers describe evidence as 'compelling' and 'rigorous.' High agreement on claims C3, C4, C76-C78, C83, C85, though peer review also includes C84, C86.

Both support chromosome pairing defects in hybrids. OpenEval emphasizes detailed cytological analysis showing ~0.7% endoreplication at pachytene vs 100% at diplotene (C62, C66). Peer reviewers accept findings on aberrant pairing (C5, C51, C59, C102) and describe cytogenetic work as 'beautiful,' though they focus more on C115-C116 regarding male arrest.

Both support the endoreplication rescue mechanism. OpenEval details the pachytene-diplotene transition with immunofluorescence data (C54-C55, C61, C103-C104). Peer review R3 explicitly endorses 'premeiotic genome endoreplication is the mechanism behind asexually-reproducing females' with strong evidence. Substantial overlap on mechanism claims C6, C54-C55, C61, C66-C67, C103-C104.

Both support cytological characterization of hybrids using flow cytometry, histology, and chromosome analysis. OpenEval cites 244 analyzed cells (C48-C52, C107, C113-C114). Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of 'impressively detailed characterization of gametogenesis.' Strong agreement on C48-C50, C113-C114.

Perfect claim overlap (C71-C75, C108-C109, C119). OpenEval provides specific statistics (z-values, p-values), peer reviewers note 'analyses are sound' and highlight 'previously overlooked effect of chromosome organisation on speciation.'

Both support low endoreplication frequency at pachytene with selective progression to diplotene. OpenEval emphasizes statistical comparisons (GLM, p-values) and 792 analyzed oocytes showing 0% in parentals (C62-C69, C121-C122). Peer review accepts quantitative findings and comparison with natural clones as 'convincing.' Overlap on C62-C65, C121-C122.

OpenEval cites experimental data showing pattern doesn't depend on particular parental genome (C8-C9, C22, C90-C91, C93-C94, C126). Peer reviewers endorse framework as providing 'important insights' about 'potential for asexuality to evolve during a relatively wide window of species divergence.' Partial overlap on C8-C9, C126.

Peer reviewers accept this framework as foundation for experimental design, praising approach of 'analysing meiotic processes across different levels of divergence.' Agreement on C34-C38.

Perfect agreement on C56, C58, C82.

OpenEval notes mechanistic interpretation involves inference from correlational data. Peer review R15 explicitly highlights 'previously overlooked effect of chromosome organisation on speciation' as central to explaining rarity of asexual lineages.

OpenEval notes mechanistic interpretation is inferential and transplantation data from cited study. Peer reviewers accept as part of overall findings on 'effect of chromosome organisation on speciation.'
